blocks.title: Guidance overview
blocks.content:
WHO TOOLKIT FOR ANALYSIS AND USE OF ROUTINE HEALTH FACILITY DATA 
This document is part of the WHO Toolkit for analysis and use of routine health facility data – a set of capacity-
building resources to optimize the analysis and use of data collected from health facilities through routine health 
information systems (RHIS). The Toolkit is a collaborative effort by multiple WHO technical programmes and 
partners. It promotes an integrated, standards-based approach to facility data analysis, using a limited set of 
standardized core indicators with recommended analyses, visualizations and dashbo

summary.text: Places the document within WHO's Toolkit for analysis and use of routine health facility data, which promotes standardized core indicators, analyses and dashboards across programmes. It describes the toolkit's components and explains that this guidance offers district and facility managers examples of using routine data for decisions, without covering district management in full.

blocks.title: Learning objectives
blocks.content:
This guidance illustrates integrated analysis of RHIS data at district and facility levels. It aims to build understanding 
and skills in a recommended analytic approach that: 
	y	
focuses on a minimum set of indicators organized into three cross-cutting groups; 
	y	
uses standard visualizations to facilitate data interpretation: charts and tables organized into integrated 
dashboards that can be automatically updated in an electronic database;  
	y	
supports use of dashboards for decision-making as part of district meetings, supervision visits and feedback 
to health facilities.  
The guida

summary.text: States the learning objectives of the guidance: a focused set of indicators in three groups, standard visualizations in integrated dashboards and their use in meetings and supervision. It defines the target audience of district managers and analysts and lists suggested reading.

blocks.title: District health system
blocks.content:
Districts are administrative units. They come in all shapes and sizes, from a few thousand people to multi-million 
populations. In many countries, districts are the main subnational administrative unit and the level that manages 
the public health service delivery system.
According to the WHO, the district health system [5] is “a network of primary care health facilities that deliver a 
comprehensive range of promotive, preventive and curative health care services to a defined population with active 
participation of the community and under the supervision of a district hospital1 and district

summary.text: Describes the district health system as a network of primary care facilities under a district hospital and management team, possibly including private providers, and explains how the term is used in the guidance.

blocks.title: Data needs of district and facility managers
blocks.content:
District and facility managers are responsible for ensuring that the health services under their management are 
appropriately delivered. This may include ensuring that:  
	y	
district health services are in line with national and subnational policies, priorities and standards;
	y	
district health services quickly detect and respond to unusual events and changing needs; 
	y	
all segments of the district population have access to the health services they need, at the required standards 
of quality;
	y	
district health services achieve required targets; and 
	y	
the resources needed to provide

summary.text: Lists the responsibilities of district and facility managers, such as meeting policies, responding to events, ensuring access and using resources efficiently, and their need for routine data and context to fulfil them.

blocks.title: Data sources at subnational level
blocks.content:
This guidance focuses on aggregate data reported through the RHIS. However, at district and facility levels, health 
information may be available from various sources as part of the broader country health information system 
(HIS). The HIS brings together data from multiple sources, including the RHIS, health facility assessments, client 
experience surveys, household surveys, censuses, civil registration systems, surveillance systems, and other 
administrative data sources [6]1. 
Various data sources are mentioned briefly in the following section; some are needed for calculation of some of 
t

summary.text: Explains that the guidance focuses on aggregate routine health information system data while noting other sources within the broader health information system, such as surveys, censuses and surveillance.

blocks.title: Routine health information system (RHIS)
blocks.content:
Health facilities routinely collect data on the diseases and other health conditions for which people seek care. 
They also collect routine data on facility activities (outputs such as number of outpatient department visits, 
number of vaccine doses given) and the outcomes of those activities (e.g. number of tuberculosis (TB) patients 
cured, number of inpatient deaths). These data are aggregated and reported at regular intervals through the 
RHIS to higher levels of the health system. Data should be analysed and used at all levels. While RHIS data are 
commonly reported each month, the freque

summary.text: Describes the routine data that health facilities collect and report on diseases, service outputs and outcomes, and how often they are reported. It also outlines related information systems, including surveillance, human resources, logistics and financial management systems.

blocks.title: Population data
blocks.content:
Population data serve as denominators for many RHIS indicators, e.g. utilization rates, coverage. It is important 
that all managers and analysts have an estimate of the population that the district system is expected to cover. 
However, there are often challenges in obtaining reliable population data. Population estimates based on 
projections of census data may be out-of-date or inaccurate; in general, the smaller the geographic area, the less 
reliable the population data. Especially challenging is the estimation of the population living in the “catchment 
area” of an individual health faci

summary.text: Discusses the difficulty of obtaining reliable population denominators, especially for facility catchment areas, and recommends analyses that avoid them, such as trends in absolute numbers and facility-based denominators. It also notes other information sources that help interpret district data.

blocks.title: Principles of this guidance
blocks.content:
This guidance is based on concepts and indicators presented in the Toolkit documents General principles and 
Integrated health services analysis: national level. 
These documents include detailed discussions on data analysis concepts and individual indicators. The focus of 
the district and facility level guidance is on practical data analysis needs at these operational levels of the health 
system. The data analysis approach of this guidance is based on five principles, listed in Box 1. 
Box 1: Principles of this guidance

summary.text: Introduces the five principles behind the guidance, building on the toolkit's general principles and national-level documents.

1.4.1 Integration – across programmes and services 
To make informed decisions, district managers need data that reflect performance across a wide range of domains 
and programmes: from coverage of immunization to utilization of financial resources. In this guidance, integrated 
analysis refers to the presentation of indicators from these multiple domains and programmes in ways that they 
can be reviewed together easily. Th

summary.text: Explains the principles of integration across programmes and of focusing on a limited set of tracer indicators to flag problems. It also discusses keeping disaggregation manageable to protect data quality, noting that WHO does not recommend sex disaggregation of routine childhood immunization data.

blocks.title: Standardization - of indicators, analyses and visualizations
blocks.content:
Standardization of data elements and indicators enables comparison over time and among places, populations and 
programmes. The way the indicators are visualized can also be standardized: a set of standard charts, tables, etc. can be 
defined and grouped in a standard dashboard. 
This document presents a sample set of standard dashboards for integrated health services analysis. There are 
dashboards for two analysis levels (health facility and district) and two timeframes (monthly and annual). Section 1.5 
discusses ways of visualizing data with charts and tables. Section 1.6 introduces the sa

summary.text: Describes standardizing indicators, analyses and visualizations so data can be compared, and introduces sample dashboards for facility and district levels over monthly and annual timeframes. It warns against cluttered electronic dashboards and stresses assessing and acknowledging data quality alongside analysis.

blocks.title: Purpose-oriented analysis - for management and planning
blocks.content:
The purpose of RHIS data is to facilitate management decision-making. This guidance offers recommendations for 
analysis of RHIS data to support decisions taken at district and facility levels. Analysis of data from recent months 
should inform short-term decisions, while review of year-to-year trends helps to guide longer-term planning. 
Table 1.1 provides a framework summarizing these types of analyses and presents some examples of management 
actions informed by each type of analysis.
Note that some of the long-term analyses relate to health resources; these analyses, while drawing upon RHI

summary.text: Explains that routine data should inform short-term decisions from recent months and longer-term planning from yearly trends, with a framework table linking analysis types to management actions such as redeploying resources or adjusting supervision.

blocks.title: Analysis, interpretation and communication of RHIS findings
Ways to analyse RHIS data
blocks.content:
Raw data are rarely suitable for decision-making. They cannot be interpreted easily and may even be misleading. 
First, the data should be “cleaned” – reviewed for completeness and consistency and, where possible, corrected. 
The data can then be visualized and analysed using charts and tables to enable easy identification and interpretation 
of key findings. 
Most analyses involve some form of comparison:  comparison over time (e.g. trends in malaria deaths); comparison 
between diseases (e.g. cases of malaria versus cases of pneumonia); comparison among health facilities (e.g. 
antenatal cli

summary.text: Explains how to clean routine data and analyse it through comparisons over time, between diseases, among facilities and against populations or targets. It describes suitable charts and tables for answering questions of when, who, what and where, with guidance on interpreting trends and outliers. A country example from Sierra Leone shows how simple tracking of immunization at facility level improved measles coverage.

blocks.title: Interpretation and communication of RHIS data findings - regular review meetings and dashboar
blocks.content:
review meetings and dashboard dissemination
It may be possible for a small number of dedicated workers in the district health office and in each facility to 
complete all the tasks described in this guidance: data quality assurance; configuration of the charts and tables; 
review and interpretation of the dashboards; further investigations; and decision-making. However, involvement 
of a wider range of staff and partners will help to ensure understanding of the RHIS data by all these stakeholders 
and will facilitate implementation of decisions based on the data. 
It is important to understand

summary.text: Describes how regular district review meetings and the distribution of printed dashboards can involve a wide range of staff in interpreting routine data. It covers meeting participants, preparation and follow-up, and ways of sending dashboards to facilities and managers as feedback.

blocks.title: Introduction to the sample dashboards and database
Lupara district database
blocks.content:
This guidance provides sample dashboards for a fictitious district called “Lupara”, created in an Excel database, the 
“Lupara district database”. The dashboards are available in Annexes 1 to 9.
The Lupara district database was created for several reasons: 
	y	
to demonstrate a comprehensive set of RHIS dashboards for district and facility levels that include most of the 
sample indicators for integrated health services analysis;  
	y	
to demonstrate recommended visualizations and good practice for presenting data; and
	y	
to use in capacity-building materials and exercises.
The database cont

summary.text: Introduces the fictitious "Lupara" district Excel database used to demonstrate the sample dashboards, explaining that its data are adapted and do not represent any real place or good data quality. It describes the dashboard naming scheme by level, timeframe and indicator group. The section ends with review questions asking readers to compare different dashboards.

blocks.title: About the data
blocks.content:
Institutional mortality refers to deaths that occur while patients are admitted in hospitals and other inpatient 
facilities.
In many countries, most deaths occur outside of health facilities, because of access challenges such as distance 
and lack of transport, as well as cultural, legal, security and financial issues. Civil registration and vital statistics 
(CRVS) systems are the official source of mortality information in a country or an administrative unit such as a 
district. However, these systems are under-developed in many contexts and other than estimates derived from 
population-bas

summary.text: Explains that institutional mortality data are often the only mortality source where civil registration is weak, while cautioning that they reflect the types of cases facilities receive. It stresses accurate cause-of-death recording using ICD coding.

The cause of death should be based on the final diagnosis, as this may be different from the admission diagnosis. 
Furthermore, the cause of death should be attributed to the underlying rather than the immediate cause. Mortality 
data should be disaggregated by sex and by at least the two age groups of 0–4 years and 5+ years.

It discusses indicators such as stillbirths, neonatal and maternal deaths, case fatality rates and perioperative mortality. The section ends with factors affecting emergency unit mortality and the need to investigate unexpected rises.

blocks.title: About the data
blocks.content:
Institutional morbidity refers to the diseases and health conditions for which people seek care at outpatient 
departments (OPD) or for which they are admitted to inpatient departments (IPD). 
Facility-based morbidity data have some similar limitations to mortality data. A large percentage of cases may 
not seek care in health facilities; therefore, facility morbidity data do not represent the true disease burden in 
the community. Also, in some contexts, many episodes of disease may be managed at pharmacies or by informal 
providers or self-medicated, and so are never recorded or reported. Ne

summary.text: Explains that facility morbidity data do not capture the full disease burden but can show patterns, and describes how diagnoses are coded and collected for outpatient and inpatient care.

blocks.content:

	y	
morbidity due to specific conditions: the numbers of cases of selected diseases or conditions.

The leading causes of morbidity (or “top 10”) analysis shows the most common diseases and conditions for which 
people seek care at a health facility. 
1. Leading inpatient discharge diagnoses and 2. Leading outpatient diagnoses 
Each indicator provides a ranked list of the 10 to 20 most common

summary.text: Describes analysing leading causes of morbidity through ranked top-10 lists of outpatient and inpatient diagnoses, counting only new outpatient cases. It also covers tracking cases of selected diseases under surveillance to spot outbreaks. Charts from the fictitious district illustrate both analyses with interpretation questions.

blocks.title: About the data
blocks.content:
Service utilization1 refers to how often people use health services. Access refers to whether people are able to 
reach health services and use them. 
Access may be influenced by many factors such as availability and functionality of services, distances to facilities, 
cultural issues or financial barriers (e.g. out-of-pocket expenses for services and transport). Utilization is often used 
to provide a rough indication (or proxy measure) of access. However, it involves more than the ability to access 
services: it also reflects whether people choose to use the services. This section discusses

summary.text: Explains the concepts of health service utilization and access for a WHO guide on analysing routine health facility data, noting that utilization is often used as a rough proxy for access. It introduces three ways of analysing utilization and service availability data. Worked examples from the fictional Lupara district show outpatient visits by age and sex, with questions for the reader.

blocks.title: Core analysis
blocks.content:
1. Outpatient service utilization/outpatient attendance per capita 
Where there is a reliable estimate of the population (such as at district level), utilization can be measured in terms 
of outpatient visits per capita (i.e. per person in the population). There is no benchmark for this indicator [14].1 
It is determined by many factors, including access to a network of facilities, supply of medicines and consumables, 
availability of laboratory and other diagnostic services, and perceptions of quality of care. However, changes over 
time should be monitored.
Fig. 3.6 (DA. 3.1 of the D 5y UCQ

summary.text: Presents core analyses of service utilization, starting with outpatient visits per capita, for which no benchmark exists but trends should be monitored, illustrated with five years of Lupara district data. Further indicators include emergency unit use, inpatient utilization, surgical volume and service-specific availability. A map shows the hospitals providing caesarean sections, with dot size proportional to the number performed in 2019.

blocks.title: About the data
blocks.content:
This section discusses data on the coverage for essential health services or, where reliable denominators are not 
available, the outputs of these services. Coverage refers to the percentage of a target population that received a 
specific health intervention or service. In this document, service output refers to the absolute number of people 
that received the intervention or service or diagnosis. The reported number of service outputs is used as a proxy for 
service coverage or, in the cases of diagnoses, the percentage of cases detected out of all cases in the community. 
While coverage ind

summary.text: Defines service coverage and service outputs and explains that reported outputs can serve as proxies for coverage where reliable population denominators are lacking. It distinguishes coverage from quality indicators and explains why PMTCT testing is classed as a quality measure in this guidance.

blocks.title: Core analysis
blocks.content:
The indicators presented here represent a sample set of tracers for coverage. (Some of these indicators do not use 
population estimates as the denominator, for the reasons discussed.) 
1. Antenatal client visits 
WHO recommends that pregnant women should have eight ANC visits, starting in the first trimester. As discussed 
in the quality section following, the reported number of ANC first visits can serve as a denominator for calculating 
indicators of ANC service quality. In systems where reliable individual patient-based data are available, the 
numbers of fourth and eighth ANC visits can a

summary.text: Describes a sample set of tracer coverage indicators, beginning with antenatal visits in line with WHO's recommendation of eight contacts starting in the first trimester. Other tracers include institutional deliveries, immunization and the detection of conditions such as hypertension and diabetes. Questions direct readers to interpret trends on the sample Lupara facility dashboards.

It notes that readmissions can signal inadequate care and that adequate resources are a prerequisite for quality services.

blocks.title: About the data
blocks.content:
Health service quality refers to how well the service is delivered, i.e. whether it is provided according to required 
standards. Service quality is a critical component of UHC – without quality, coverage will not be effective and UHC 
cannot be achieved.  
Measuring quality is important both because the quality of a service or specific intervention determines its 
effectiveness and because community perceptions of quality influence service utilization and coverage. Quality 
assessment involves comparing actual service provision to an agreed standard of “good quality”. Measurement 
may be comp

summary.text: Defines health service quality as delivery according to required standards and explains its importance for universal health coverage, noting that quality has many dimensions. It states that the section covers process and outcome indicators, with resource indicators left to the next chapter.

blocks.title: Core analysis
blocks.content:
1. Antenatal client 1st visit before 12 weeks’ gestation (%)
This indicator assesses community awareness of the importance of an early start to ANC care. WHO recommends 
that ANC starts in the first trimester (before reaching 12 weeks of pregnancy), to allow early detection of problems 
and to promote the best possible outcomes for both mother and baby. Health education and support starting 
early in pregnancy also help to promote a positive pregnancy experience for the woman. 
2. PMTCT testing (%) and 3. Intermittent preventive treatment for malaria during pregnancy (IPTp3) %
These two indica

summary.text: Works through core quality indicators, explaining what each reveals, such as early antenatal care, PMTCT testing and malaria preventive treatment in pregnancy. Others include caesarean section rates, immunization dropout and the HIV care cascade, plus inpatient and malaria case management measures. A Lupara district table of values ends with a question asking readers to spot suspicious findings, such as treatment percentages above 100%.

blocks.title: About the data
blocks.content:
Resources (inputs or production factors) are necessary to provide health services. The main inputs for health 
service delivery include health facilities (infrastructure), equipment, staff, medicines and medical products, and 
financial resources. Financial resources are converted into the other resources or used in monetary form, for 
example, to cover operational costs. 
Information on the availability and use of these resources can provide insights into health service performance, 
including the indicators described in the previous chapters of this guidance. 
The measurement of health resou

summary.text: Explains that resources such as facilities, equipment, staff, medicines and finance are needed to deliver services and that resource data can shed light on performance. It notes that such data are often held outside routine information systems, for example in administrative and finance databases.

blocks.title: Core analysis
blocks.content:
 Infrastructure and equipment: availability and distribution
1. Health facility density and distribution 
A facility network refers to the health facilities serving a defined population and functioning under a health 
management team, e.g. a district network. The network is composed of all the PHC facilities and the secondary 
(referral) facilities of the district. While private, NGO and other facilities are not under the responsibility of the 
district health management team, these facilities should be included in density indicators to understand the overall 
availability of services – and e

summary.text: Presents core analyses of health service resources, starting with facility density and distribution drawn from a master facility list, and hospital bed density. Further indicators assess efficiency through bed occupancy and length of stay, as well as health workforce availability and medicine stock-outs. The section ends with health finance, asking readers to interpret Lupara district's 2019 budget execution and plan spending for the last quarter.

blocks.title: Annex 10: Answers to the questions in the guidance document
blocks.content:
guidance document
Question 1: There was a sudden rise in the institutional mortality rate in December 2019. Institutional mortality 
was also high from June to September, although not as high as in December and, as is explained for some other 
charts, a mid-year rise in mortality during the mid-year “sick season” for Lupara district is expected from review 
of data for previous years.

summary.text: Annex 10 gives model answers to the exercise questions throughout the routine health facility data guidance, based on the Lupara district dashboards. Early answers interpret patterns such as a December spike in institutional mortality and the age and sex distribution of outpatient visits. Later answers address coverage, quality and resource indicators, including data quality concerns. The last answer advises limiting fourth-quarter spending to essential activities given budget execution.
